transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Park (Redwood SE), Maya Liu (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (TideLake CTO), Ben Ortiz (Head of ML), Ravi Menon (Infra Eng), Laura Chen (Product)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): TideLake evaluating dedicated GPUs for inference. Key asks: isolation, burst capacity, predictable latency, and ability to run pilot/benchmarks. Security and KMS questions surfaced.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Samir from Redwood. Quick intro from our side, Jules and Maya are on the call to cover technical and security questions.
[00:12] Aisha: Hi, thanks. I'll let Ben kick off on what we're trying to solve.
[00:16] Ben: Sure. So high level, we're TideLake, we run risk-scoring and customer support automations. We're exploring moving some inference off our current self-hosted clusters into a dedicated provider setup that gives us reserved GPUs but also network isolation — we have PCI-ish constraints. Our key goals are predictable throughput and tight p95 latency under load.
[00:34] Jules: Got it. When you say reserved GPUs, are you thinking single-tenant hardware or dedicated tenants in a shared cluster?
[00:41] Ben: Prefer single-tenant pools if possible. We need logical isolation and no co-tenancy for certain models. But curious about Redwood's Dedicated offering — how isolation is enforced and what the burst model looks like.
[00:52] Samir: Great, Redwood Dedicated is reserved capacity — you get a GPU pool dedicated to your org. We support VPC peering and private endpoints; for on-prem style needs we also offer Private deployments but sounds like Dedicated with VPC might fit. For isolation we can do customer-dedicated nodes and network isolation with no shared compute.
[01:12] Ravi: Quick Q on storage: we keep KV caches and some model artifacts in a shared object store normally. How do you handle that without leaking data?
[01:19] Maya: Good question. For Dedicated we can provision a customer-specific object store or encrypt items with customer KMS keys. We support integration with AWS KMS and HSM-based stores; audit logs capture access to KV cache and model loads.
[01:33] Laura: What's the SLA look like? We need a 99.9% uptime target for inference.
[01:38] Samir: Our Dedicated SLAs can be contractually set — 99.9% is commonly requested. We'll map out failover options: multi-az placements and automatic fallback to a compatible model in another pool if needed.
[01:52] Ben: Cost is a big factor. How do we think about reserved vs burst pricing? We have spiky nightly loads for batch scoring and steady interactive traffic during the day.
[02:01] Jules: We typically recommend sizing for baseline interactive QPS and then enabling burst capacity or autoscaling for nightly batches. Burst can be pre-purchased (burst credits) or on-demand; reserved capacity gives a lower unit price for steady usage.
[02:18] Aisha: Is there throttling or queueing? We need p95 latency under 300ms for inference calls at 95th percentile.
[02:26] Samir: Latency targets depend on model choice and sequence length. For short prompts on quantized models we commonly hit sub-200ms p95 on our low-latency profiles. For longer contexts or larger models, you may need bigger GPUs or more instances dedicated to concurrency.
[02:42] Ben: We're using a 4k token context for some tasks, but for customer support completions it's more like 1k tokens. We also make heavy use of embeddings for similarity search.
[02:52] Jules: That helps. For 4k contexts you want to avoid small GPU types; memory and kv-cache handling matter. We'll recommend instance types and a batching strategy — continuous batching for throughput, but we can tune max latency.
[03:06] Ravi: How does autoscaling behave with reserved pools — can it burst into shared capacity if we spike beyond the reservation?
[03:12] Samir: Yes, policy-driven. You can configure a primary reserved pool and a fallback that can be either your own burst pool or our shared hosted pool with data handling rules. If you need strict isolation, fallback can still be into a pre-provisioned private burst pool. If you accept some shared compute for bursts, costs are lower.
[03:30] Laura: We want to avoid any risk of PII leaving our VPC. Is there a way to keep data entirely in our network?
[03:36] Maya: With Dedicated + VPC peering and customer-managed KMS, data in transit is over your private link. For the strictest cases, our Private deployment brings the control plane into your VPC or on-prem. Many customers start with Dedicated and move to Private if they need air-gapped requirements.
[03:55] Ben: On performance testing — can you run a benchmark using our representative prompt set? We want real-world p95 numbers and token cost estimates.
[04:03] Samir: Absolutely. Best practice: you provide 24h traces and representative prompts; we run a benchmark on a reserved pilot pool mirroring production config. That gives latency percentiles, throughput, and cost per 1,000 tokens.
[04:16] Ben: Timeline-wise, how fast can a pilot spin up?
[04:19] Samir: For Dedicated pilot, we can spin a pool in ~5 business days if it's standard region/cloud. Private deployments take longer.
[04:26] Aisha: Security and compliance — SOC2, ISO, and audit logs are must-haves. Also SSO/SAML for admin access.
[04:33] Jules: We have SOC2 reports and ISO artifacts; we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and log streaming to your SIEM. I'll attach the security docs after the call.
[04:44] Ravi: One more infra nit — what's the expected ops surface for us? Do we manage model versioning or do you?
[04:50] Maya: We provide a model catalog and versioning for served models. Customers can pin model versions, roll back, and we support canary and A/B rollouts. For some customers we also do managed model ops as an add-on.
[05:04] Ben: For scaling, we expect to grow from ~50 QPS peak now to 500 QPS within 6 months if experiments succeed. Any sizing rules of thumb?
[05:13] Jules: Rough rule: model family and quantization determine tokens/sec per GPU. We'll give you concrete numbers in the sizing sheet, but initial recommendation is a combo of n1 GPUs for low latency plus a few higher-memory GPUs for long-context jobs. Also use caching for prefixes that repeat a lot — that reduces token compute.
[05:33] Aisha: Ok, costs and contract length — do you do monthly reserved or annual only?
[05:38] Samir: We support monthly reserved capacity (with higher unit price) and discounted annual commitments. There's also the option to start with a short pilot credits package.
[05:47] Laura: Any competitors or migration pitfalls we should be aware of?
[05:50] Samir: Common competitors are big cloud offerings and API-native players; migration pitfalls are usually around prompt engineering differences, tokenization differences, and hidden network latencies. We run evals and alignment tests to spot regressions.
[06:05] Ben: Can you show a quick sketch of the recommended burst policy?
[06:09] Jules: Sure — (Jules shares screen, described) Primary reserved pool sized for 150 QPS, autoscale policy with threshold at 70% CPU/GPU util, burst pool pre-warmed to 200% capacity but billed as burst credits and capped to avoid runaway costs. Fallback route to hosted pool with data redaction rules if isolation isn't required.
[06:33] Ravi: Are there quotas for concurrent KV cache entries? We need large stateful sessions for a small subset of users.
[06:39] Maya: We support session affinity and large KV caches on dedicated nodes; we can size memory and disk based on your session retention settings.
[06:49] Aisha: Ok, let's talk pilot success criteria — what does success look like to Redwood?
[06:54] Samir: For a pilot: achieve p95 latency targets specified by you, validate no data leakage, demonstrate predictable unit costs, and confirm autoscale/burst behavior under your workloads.
[07:06] Ben: Great. I'm going to put a few requests — we'll send traces and 5 prompt families. Also need pricing per model family and recommended instance types.
[07:14] Samir: Perfect. We'll follow up with the sizing/pricing worksheet and security docs.
[07:19] Laura: Anything else from Redwood side?
[07:21] Jules: I'll prepare the SOC2/ISO attachments and a short runbook for the pilot.
[07:25] Maya: And I'll add notes on KMS integration and our recommended caching config.
[07:29] Aisha: Ok, timeline — can we aim to start the pilot the week of March 16th?
[07:33] Samir: Yes, that lines up. I'll confirm availability and send calendar invite with baseline agenda.
[07:38] Ben: Cool. One last Q — can you give a rough token cost delta for using a quantized model vs a full FP? Ballpark is fine.
[07:44] Jules: Ballpark, quantized models can reduce per-token compute by 30-60% depending on precision and kernel support. We'll put estimated $/1k token numbers in the pricing sheet.
[07:55] Samir: Alright, thanks everyone. We'll recap next steps in an email.

Meeting recap (auto): next steps and owners above. Action items: pricing and security docs from Redwood; traces and prompts from TideLake; schedule benchmark.
